content: The uranyl ion is a positively charged cation with a charge of +2, which forms salts when combined with acids. In this ion, uranium exists in its +6 oxidation state. Another common oxidation state of uranium is uranium(IV), also known as uranous. The uranyl ion is the most frequently encountered species in the aqueous chemistry of uranium. Solid uranyl compounds are often visually identifiable by their red, yellow, orange, or green coloration. Like all uranium compounds, uranyl compounds are toxic, with soluble uranyl salts being particularly hazardous due to their rapid incorporation into biological tissues. Examples of uranyl compounds include uranium trioxide (UO₃), uranyl acetate (UO₂(C₂H₃O₂)₂), uranyl ammonium carbonate (UO₂CO₃·2(NH₄)₂CO₃), uranyl carbonate (UO₂CO₃), uranyl chloride (UO₂Cl₂), uranyl hydroxide (UO₂(OH)₂ or (UO₂)₂(OH)₂ in aqueous form), uranyl nitrate (UO₂(NO₃)₂), uranyl sulfate (UO₂SO₄), and uranyl zinc acetate (ZnUO₂(CH₃COO)₄). Uranyl minerals are typically found in the oxidized portions of uranium ore deposits. Common uranyl minerals include tyuyamunite (Ca(UO₂)₂V₂O₈·8H₂O), autunite (Ca(UO₂)₂(PO₄)₂·8-12H₂O), torbernite (Cu(UO₂)₂(PO₄)·8-12H₂O), and uranophane ((H₃O)₂Ca(UO₂)₂(SiO₄)·3H₂O). These minerals, which contain uranium in the +6 oxidation state, provide valuable insights into the formation of uranium deposits and the interactions between water and rock in uranium-rich mineral seams. The chemistry of uranium has traditionally focused on the aqueous chemistry of the uranyl ion and related molecular species. One significant application of this chemistry is the preparation of uranium dioxide ceramic pellets, which serve as fuel in light water nuclear reactors. However, the chemical degradation of these fuel materials often begins before the uranium is fully consumed, and this degradation process is an active area of research. Many of the corrosion products formed during this process belong to the uranyl group. The structure of the uranyl ion has been a topic of extensive scientific debate. The short U=O bonds in the uranyl ion have been attributed to d-p and f-p bonding interactions, which prevent the close approach of additional ligands beyond the two axial oxygen atoms. Uranyl nitrate is a highly toxic and oxidizing compound that should never be ingested. Exposure to uranyl nitrate can cause severe renal insufficiency, acute tubular necrosis, and acts as a lymphocyte mitogen. The primary target organs for uranyl ion toxicity include the kidneys, liver, lungs, and brain. Accumulation of uranyl ions in tissues, including gonocytes, can lead to congenital disorders, while their presence in white blood cells can result in immune system damage. Additionally, uranyl compounds are known neurotoxins. The aerial oxidation of any uranium compound eventually leads to the formation of a uranyl compound. Contamination by uranyl ions has been detected on and around depleted uranium targets, highlighting the environmental and health risks associated with uranium combustion and its byproducts.
